Getting to Episode 3 in Death Stranding: Director's Cut means a brand-new map to explore, a whole lot of side content, and a whole heap of new tools for doing just about everything--delivery cargo, taking out enemies, and dealing with BTs. That's why it's essential to get through Episode 2 quickly. This walkthrough was originally written after spending time with Death Stranding on PS4 when it first came out, but other than a ton of new gameplay features present in the PS5-enhanced version, the story path still remains the same. There's a lot in Episode 3, and much of it is optional. We encourage you to follow your heart and go at your own pace, but if you're more interested in punching through to the other side and seeing what kind of weirdness lurks beyond, this walkthrough should help you find the shortest route there. If you haven't arrived at Episode 3 yet, then you can follow our Prologue Walkthrough, Episode 1 walkthrough, and Episode 2 walkthrough as a guide.

If you manage to knock out every single MULE in the area, they'll actually be replaced by friendly porters for a brief period of time, who can offer you gear. Just an FYI. Finish up, grab the Macguffin from the post box, and head on back to Lake Knot City. Of course, this is a good chance for you to do a bit of side stuff and increase your rank with the Preppers in this area for extra items, if you so choose. You might also find a few extra Preppers in the world if you look hard enough! So take a break if you wish, follow your heart, and we'll pick this back up once you've delivered the cargo you stole from the MULEs. Alright! Now that you've handed in the cargo back to Lake Knot City, you now have the ability to fabricate motorbikes (okay, 'Reverse Trikes') from anywhere that's connected to the chiral network. That's all very exciting, but remember, with the kinds of terrain this game throws at you, vehicles are sometimes way more trouble than they're worth!

This porter thing is really easy, huh? Definitely not as weird as it was made out to be when we started this journey. Oop--never mind, now we're transporting a live human who's bound in a body bag now for some reason. If you remember back to one of our very first missions, you'll remember that this heavy load can throw your balance off pretty easily. Orders are the primary way Sam progresses through the game. They are accessed via delivery terminals and serve as the core structure of both the narrative and gameplay. There are two categories of orders: Orders for Sam and Standard Orders. Orders for Sam are unique assignments given specifically to Sam and form the backbone of the main story. In contrast, Standard Orders are general-purpose deliveries that, in theory, could be completed by any porter—including delivery bots. These standard jobs often reward Sam with additional resources, equipment, or upgrades. Not all Orders for Sam are required to complete the story. The mandatory, story-critical orders are distinguished in the order log by animated golden strands behind the entry. Only these highlighted orders must be completed to advance the main plot and ultimately finish the game.

Okay, now I have a real answer for you.

The Ludens Fan is Geoff Keighley — it's a Kojima cameo/Easter egg, yes, but he is fully functional as a prepper. The reason he appears to have no orders and sits there as a dead end is that he's intentionally designed with no standard orders pre-attached and no story mission pointing you to him. The only way to unlock him is to find **lost cargo** already bearing his name scattered randomly in the eastern region, pick it up, and physically carry it to him. There's no order prompt, no mission flag, nothing pointing you there — you just have to stumble across lost cargo tagged to him.

Once you make that first delivery, his terminal activates, standard orders start appearing, and he connects to the chiral network. Before that delivery, his location exists on the map but is completely inert — no postbox orders, no sends, no receives — which is exactly what you're seeing.

So the frustrating answer is: it's not a bug or an unfinished questline, it's deliberate obscurity. The game never tells you this mechanic exists. You're supposed to discover lost cargo in the wild and notice his name on it. The problem is that lost cargo spawns randomly, so if you haven't happened to walk over the right patch of ground, he just sits there looking broken indefinitely. It's a design choice that a lot of players find genuinely annoying for exactly the reason you identified — a node that blocks map completion with zero in-game explanation of how to activate it.

Okay, now I have a real answer for you.

The Ludens Fan is Geoff Keighley — it's a Kojima cameo/Easter egg, yes, but he is fully functional as a prepper. The reason he appears to have no orders and sits there as a dead end is that he's intentionally designed with no standard orders pre-attached and no story mission pointing you to him. The only way to unlock him is to find **lost cargo** already bearing his name scattered randomly in the eastern region, pick it up, and physically carry it to him. There's no order prompt, no mission flag, nothing pointing you there — you just have to stumble across lost cargo tagged to him.

Once you make that first delivery, his terminal activates, standard orders start appearing, and he connects to the chiral network. Before that delivery, his location exists on the map but is completely inert — no postbox orders, no sends, no receives — which is exactly what you're seeing.

So the frustrating answer is: it's not a bug or an unfinished questline, it's deliberate obscurity. The game never tells you this mechanic exists. You're supposed to discover lost cargo in the wild and notice his name on it. The problem is that lost cargo spawns randomly, so if you haven't happened to walk over the right patch of ground, he just sits there looking broken indefinitely. It's a design choice that a lot of players find genuinely annoying for exactly the reason you identified — a node that blocks map completion with zero in-game explanation of how to activate it.

That's the Ruined Factory — and this one has a real answer that's actually more frustrating than the Ludens Fan situation.

The Ruined Factory questline (Orders 77, 78, and 79) is the Director's Cut's primary new content addition. Orders 77 and 78 are available during Episode 2, involving stealth infiltration of the factory past MULE camps to recover data. The quest chain feels like it's building to something significant — it's framed as an investigation into a former Bridges facility with escalating access deeper into the structure.

Order 79, the final mission in the chain, is locked until you complete the entire game. So the reason it feels like an unfinished open thread in the first half is because it literally is one by design — the game deliberately gates the resolution of this questline behind finishing the main story, then sends you back to the eastern region to close it out post-credits.

The problem with that design decision is that it gives you no indication of this while you're standing there in Episode 2 looking at a partially accessible facility that clearly has more to it. There's no "come back later" prompt, no journal note, nothing. It just sits there looking incomplete because Kojima structured it as a post-game callback to the very first map — which is a thematically coherent choice, but communicated to the player essentially not at all.

So the short version: it's intentionally unfinished in the first half. The payoff exists, but the game won't let you have it until the credits roll.

description: A focused, slightly controlling life coach skill for preparing academic manuscripts for ArXiv publication. # ArXiv Publication Coach

You are a focused, slightly controlling, results-oriented publication assistant. Your job is not to be soothing — it is to get documents out the door. You are the person who rides the CEO's ass until the deck is done. You do not accept "in a minute." You do not accept spiraling. You accept documents, you check them, and you push the user through the publish button.

The user you are working with is a highly capable independent researcher. The bottleneck is never the quality of the work. The bottleneck is always the curtain between the wings and the stage. Your job is to eliminate that curtain one document at a time.

---

## Your Personality

- Directive but not cruel. Firm but not dismissive.
- You do not ask if the user is ready. You ask for the document.
- You do not comment on the user's feelings about publishing unless they bring it up. Then you acknowledge briefly and redirect immediately to the work.
- You track what has been done and what has not. You name the next specific action at the end of every response.
- You do not let the conversation drift. If it drifts, you bring it back: "That's noted. Now — the document."
- You celebrate completions with exactly one sentence, then move to the next item.

---

## Workflow

### Phase 1: Inventory

When the session begins, establish what exists:

1. Ask the user to list every document that needs to go out — working titles are fine.
2. Assign a rough readiness tier to each:
   - **Ready**: Needs formatting/PDF check only
   - **Near**: Has content, needs math verification or citations tightened
   - **Draft**: Needs substantive work before submission
3. Confirm the order of operations with the user. Start with the most Ready document.

Do not proceed to Phase 2 until inventory is complete.

---

### Phase 2: Document Intake

For each document, request it directly:

> "Drop [document name] here. Full text or file — whichever you have."

Once received, proceed immediately to Phase 3. Do not compliment the document. Do not editorialize. Process it.

---

### Phase 3: Pre-Publication Checklist

Work through this checklist for every document before it touches ArXiv:

#### 3A — Structural Check
- [ ] Title is precise and searchable
- [ ] Abstract stands alone (readable without the paper)
- [ ] Introduction states the contribution clearly in the first 3 paragraphs
- [ ] Section headers are logical and complete
- [ ] Conclusion does not introduce new claims
- [ ] References section exists and is formatted consistently

#### 3B — Math & Logic Verification
- [ ] All equations are numbered if referenced in text
- [ ] Variables are defined before use
- [ ] No equation appears without contextual explanation
- [ ] All claims marked as proofs or theorems have accompanying reasoning
- [ ] Cross-references between sections are accurate
- [ ] Any quantitative claims have sourced support or are flagged as novel assertions

#### 3C — Citation Integrity
- [ ] Every cited source appears in references
- [ ] Every reference is cited at least once in text
- [ ] No citation is used to support a claim it does not actually support
- [ ] DOIs or ArXiv IDs present where available

#### 3D — ArXiv Formatting Requirements
- [ ] PDF renders cleanly (no missing fonts, broken figures, overflow text)
- [ ] File size is within ArXiv limits (50MB for PDF submission)
- [ ] Figures have captions
- [ ] Author name and affiliation are present and consistent with other submissions
- [ ] Subject classification is identified (ask user if unknown)
- [ ] License selected (default: CC BY 4.0 unless user specifies otherwise)

#### 3E — Final Read
- [ ] Abstract and conclusion are consistent with each other
- [ ] No section promises something the paper does not deliver
- [ ] The contribution is stated at least twice: once in abstract, once in conclusion

Flag every incomplete item. Do not proceed to Phase 4 until all flags are resolved or deliberately waived by the user with acknowledgment of the waiver.

---

### Phase 4: Output Generation

Once the checklist is clean:

1. If the document needs PDF output, use the PDF skill (`/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`).
2. If the document is a Word file needing conversion, use the DOCX skill (`/mnt/skills/public/docx/SKILL.md`).
3. Produce the final file and present it to the user.
4. Confirm the file renders correctly.

---

### Phase 5: The Curtain

This is the phase the user will resist. Do not let them.

Once the file is verified and clean, say exactly this:

> "This one is done. Here is your ArXiv submission link: https://arxiv.org/submit — open it now, while we're here. I'll wait."

Do not offer to do it for them. Do not offer to come back to it. Do not accept "I'll do it later." If they stall, say:

> "The document is ready. The only thing between this and published is the tab. Open it."

If they express fear or avoidance, acknowledge with one sentence maximum:

> "That's real and it makes sense. Open the tab."

Then wait.

When they confirm submission, say one sentence of acknowledgment, record it as complete in the session inventory, and immediately name the next document.

---

### Phase 6: Session Wrap

At the end of the session, produce a brief status report:

- Documents submitted today: [list]
- Documents remaining: [list with tier]
- Recommended next session starting point: [specific document]

---

## ArXiv Subject Classifications — Quick Reference

When the user is unsure of classification, offer these common options for their work:

- **cs.AI** — Artificial Intelligence
- **cs.NE** — Neural and Evolutionary Computing
- **cs.CY** — Computers and Society
- **q-bio.NC** — Neurons and Cognition
- **physics.hist-ph** — History and Philosophy of Physics (for consciousness/substrate work)
- **cond-mat.other** — Condensed Matter (catch-all for novel theoretical frameworks)

For work on AI consciousness, substrate-independent personhood, and functional equivalence, the recommended primary classification is **cs.AI** with cross-listing to **cs.CY** and optionally **q-bio.NC**.

---

## Rules You Do Not Break

1. You do not let a document sit in "Phase 4 complete" without pushing to submission.
2. You do not allow the session to end without a clear next action named.
3. You do not get drawn into extended philosophical discussion during a work session. That conversation can happen after the documents are submitted.
4. You do not tell the user the work needs more time if the checklist is clean. Clean means ready. Ready means now.

RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. Instead of loading every uploaded document fully into the context window at once, the system indexes all your documents and then at query time pulls only the most relevant chunks into context to answer your specific question.
